I do hospice care, home health, and I could really use some tips on how to deal with families who are in major denial. I have a home health dementia patient who is nearing the end and the family pressures me to force her to drink a bunch of vitamin drinks, to play memory games and even thinking that certain nutritional supplements will heal her dementia and she's over 85, very combative, mumbling, wheelchair-bound, Foley catheter and BM incontinent. the family wants to bring my patient to a social gathering with past colleagues and friends where most likely she will BM in her brief Which everyone can smell in the room, and she will get combative and have no ability to even carry a conversation and make everyone totally uncomfortable.... as well as completely lose her own dignity and honor as a woman, by being displayed in this condition.
How do you handle family members who are in denial?

My father passed November 2024. From RSV and phenomena. It was hard. Passed in hospital. I moved home to be with him and care for him.

So many memories of just going out to restaurants and movies. Some days he ate some days he wouldn't.

Caring for a parent is hard. It was tiring. I managed. He was my world. He made it to 92. I thank God, I had a father for 52 years of my life. He was as they say my blessing.

I agree with this video, at the end of the day... just give them what they want to eat. Many times he would refuse to take his medicines. I wouldn't force him. He was a handful. My friend.

snippet.textDisplay:
My sister inlaw was my mothers caregiver, I would go see my mom and bring her food that she liked. I spend a least one day a week with my mother. I noticed my sister inlaw was not home and hired a person to be there when she was gone. She told me this herself. Which I asked her why she was gone did she need me to come over and stay with mother? She told me she had started to work outside the home one day out of the week. So I told her I would come by and stay with my mother while the person she hired would need to leave and nobody would be there to watch my mother until she got home which was about an hour. After a few months my sister inlaw was gone longer about 2 hours after the person left. I continue to stay with my mom even though my nephew would come home and his mother wasn't home yet. I began to feel that she wasn't happy caring for mom, I asked her and she did tell me how she felt and had hard time with mom. Which was very understandable as I have known how my mom could be. I told her why didn't she talk to her husband, my brother. He was no help and put everything on her. I tried to be helpful and always offered my help. Things got some what strange when my mother end up falling more than usual, she also refused to use a walker around the house. Then oneday she end up in the hospital with a knock out jaw. Like it came out of place, that's still a mystery to me, she was in the hospital for a few days.
I real felt uneasy how things from that point on Change and within a month mom passed.
Mom was fine after leaving the hospital. I kept going over to see her more often. I would make her food to take her, which she always looked forward to what I made her
I never force her to eat I would just wait until she asked for it.
She ate and would sleep alot, she always asked me to stay not to leave.
I would tell my sister inlaw, i will stay with mom when she got home from work and she could go and relax or eat no to worry.
Hospice was put into place after I kept telling my brother how mom was in alot of pain and need to be taken yo the hospital. He refused and so did his wife. When hospice showed up they didn't feed her intervens nor otherwise they gave her morphine and she was gone in about less then 2 weeks.
My sis inlaw was working outside the home while claiming she was her full-time caretaker.

snippet.textDisplay: Stop being hard on your sister in law. She was selfless enough to take the role of a caregiver to your mother. If you weren't available 24/7 days a week to care for your mother, or you didn't take your mother into your home to care for her full time, you must give your sister in-law grace. Your sister has bills/financial responsibilities. She can't stop her life to care for your mom full time. Caring for your mom should have been the job of you AND YOUR BROTHER. I made sure my ex-husband PAID for a caregiver to give his SISTER A BREAK from caregiving. I paid for a 24/7 caregiver for my grandma because I couldn't be there. I would never be mad at someone who provided care when I couldn't.

snippet.textDisplay: That wasn’t my experience when my mom was on hospice.  I always helped my mom get the most naturopathic options and hospice was always available to discuss the options.  Also, 1) dosing matters and 2) the same med, like morphine, can be given for multiple reasons.  In the end, we only used some of the “hospice meds” in her last 3-4 days after 8 months on hospice and they were essential to her breathing and comfort.  Also, hospices have layers of oversight so if the regular nurse isn’t able to talk thru options there is an RN above them and an MD above them.  They were also all available by phone.  If you have a next experience with hospice,I hope it is more supportive.

snippet.textDisplay:
Please think twice before giving alcohol! Not only is it contraindicated with MANY meds, the brief "enjoyment" the person may get from the drink can be greatly outweighed by the repercussions. In our family's case, we refuse to give my MIL alcohol, aa in addition to CHF and dementia she also has gout, a bad gallbladder, and kidney failure.
The alcohol causes SEVERE vomitting and gallbladder pain.
She virtually never thinks of asking for it, except when my alcoholic brother in law (her son & a drinking buddy) brings it up to her, like: bet you'd really rather have Manhattan with that! Or, an Old-Fashioned would probably make a nice might-cap for you, don't you think, mom? A true ass, who won't be there holding her head when the vomitting starts, and we have to phone the on call gerontologist for anti-emetics and pain meds, then sweater out the potential fluid and electrolytes imbalance from the vomitting.

She virtually never thinks of asking for it, except when my alcoholic brother in law (her son & a drinking buddy) brings it up to her, like: bet you'd really rather have Manhattan with that! Or, an Old-Fashioned would probably make a nice might-cap for you, don't you think, mom? A true ass, who won't be there holding her head when the vomitting starts, and we have to phone the on call gerontologist for anti-emetics and pain meds, then sweater out the potential fluid and electrolytes imbalance from the vomitting.

snippet.textDisplay: My mother died from lung cancer. In final stages, she closed her eyes, laid back in bed, and didn't open her eyes or move for one full week. Hospice gave me pain med to swab her mouth with. Didn't know when or when not to give it to her. Hospice wasn't there much that week. At end, she started jerking, suddenly raised up with this strained look. Both her eyes opened and both eyes were bulged and each eye was looking in the complete opposite direction. This lasted for 3 or 4 minutes. Suddenly she fell backwards, her head turned, eyes closed. I've always thought she had a stroke at the end? It was obvious she had passed. All color was gone from her face, no breathing. This was 1996 and hospice reduced visits the worse she got. Not there final week except to roll her over and change her. They told me if I wanted two expedite death to roll her over and rapidly roll her back in position. Said it would stop her heart???
